claims.text: A thin, controlled WC interphase at W–Cu interfaces increases the overall thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites.
A thin, controlled WC interphase allows W–Cu composites to retain mechanical durability.
A thin, controlled WC interphase allows W–Cu composites to retain irradiation resistance.
Localized carburization of the tungsten phase can form a nanometer-scale WC layer at W–Cu interfaces during composite processing.
The proposed effect should hold under moderate to high thermal loads and at temperatures up to approximately 500°C.
The proposed effect should hold at irradiation doses applicable to fusion-reactor components.
The WC interphase improves thermal coupling between the copper matrix and tungsten reinforcements.
The WC interphase improves interfacial bonding between the copper matrix and tungsten reinforcements.
The WC layer provides a more compatible bonding structure between tungsten and copper.
The more compatible bonding structure reduces thermal interface resistance.
The WC interphase decreases phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
Tungsten carbide has inherent mechanical strength that helps preserve composite mechanical durability.
Tungsten carbide has irradiation stability that helps preserve composite irradiation resistance.
The engineered composite may have approximately 20% higher thermal conductivity than a comparable conventional W–Cu composite.
The engineered composite will have mechanical durability comparable to the control.
The engineered composite will have irradiation resistance comparable to the control.
The expected benefits require a uniformly formed WC layer maintained within a controlled thickness range of a few nanometers.
A nonuniform or overgrown WC layer may introduce brittleness or excessive interphase resistance and negate the expected benefits.
